title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Course Description
Covers the fundamentals of deep learning, including important models, such as deep feedforward, recurrent, convolutional and transformer neural networks, and algorithms and considerations for training them. The application of deep learning to domains such as natural language, speech and vision will also be discussed.

title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Course Outcomes
On completion of CSCI 481, students will demonstrate:

An understanding of machine learning fundamentals.
A thorough understanding of deep feedforward neural networks.
An understanding of deep learning optimization and regularization.
An understanding of recurrent and convolutional neural networks.
The ability to implement deep learning models using modern toolkits.
The ability to conduct deep learning experiments.

title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Textbooks and readings
There are no required textbooks for the course, but several books and notes are recommended:

Deep Learning (dds), the course notes for CSCI 481.
Deep Learning [1], the main reference text. The book can be viewed at no cost from the book’s webpage.
Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction [2], ISBN 9780262046824. The author offers a free PDF on the book’s webpage.
Machine Learning with PyTorch and Scikit-Learn [3], ISBN 9781801819312. Code examples and Jupyter notebooks are available from the book’s GitHub repository.
Machine Learning for Data Science (lds), the notes for the prerequisite machine learning course.

The class will not follow one book closely; use these books and notes as references.

Communication
Outbound. I will send official class announcements through Canvas Announcements. Please set Canvas to notify you of them right away, so you do not miss important information.
Inbound. All course-related correspondence goes through Canvas. Nearly all questions or comments from you to me and/or the grader should be posted on the official class discussion forum, which is Canvas Discussions. Anything that should not be posted there, such as a grading question or objection, goes in a Canvas message to me and the grader.
The only class-related matters that should not go through Canvas at all are those containing confidential information (e.g., information about your health). Communications containing confidential information should be sent to my WWU email address, which is the one exception to using Canvas.

title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Questions and Corrections
If something in the course materials seems wrong, ask. The course materials include the notes, handouts, assignments, and anything I say or show in class, including my slides. I will make mistakes, and so will the other authors of the materials.
Do not assume that you are the confused one when the material might be wrong. Richard Feynman told a room of science teachers that “science is the belief in the ignorance of experts” [4], and in this course I am (supposedly) one of the experts. Ask your question first, in class or outside it, and we can talk through your reasoning together. If you are right, we all learn something and I fix the material. If you are not, we can jointly find out where the confusion started.

The health and safety of everyone in the class is a top priority. In short: if you are sick with something that could be communicable, let me know ahead of time and I will try to arrange a remote participation option, so you can stay home and not expose others needlessly. Please contact me if you have questions, concerns or suggestions.

title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Software
Homework is written in Python, using PyTorch. You will install PyTorch in a Python virtual environment. Expect to implement core methods yourself, first with NumPy and then with PyTorch’s building blocks, before reaching for higher-level libraries.

title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Student-Centered Teaching
Student-centered teaching methodologies, which prioritize student learning outcomes over instructor output (“more doing, less listening”), have been shown to be vastly more effective than traditional lectures. As Brian Hutchinson highlights from wearable-sensor studies of electrodermal activity [5] and his lecture presentation [6], traditional passive lectures produce low sympathetic nervous system arousal and attention—comparable to watching television and sleeping. Active problem-solving, formative assessment, and peer discussion elevate engagement and learning.
Furthermore, cognitive science shows that “the less effort it takes to learn something, the less durable that learning is” [7]. This course is intentionally challenging for the right reasons, backed by a growth mindset: talent and mathematical ability can be developed through focused effort, challenges expand your abilities, and mistakes are essential opportunities to grow. Research confirms that an instructor’s growth-mindset beliefs predict student achievement and motivation even after accounting for other faculty characteristics [8].
Each lecture is built from exercises: I pose a question, you work on it alone or in a small group, and then we discuss solutions together.

ABCD Cards
On the first day of class, I will give each student an ABCD card, which you will use to vote on answers to questions in class. They work like electronic clickers, but they are free and need no batteries. I use them because they allow both you and me to quickly assess how well you understand the material, so that I can adjust what I emphasize in class and you can adjust what you study out of class to improve learning outcomes. Please bring this card to class each day.

Homework
The course has five graded homework assignments, as well as additional ungraded exercises and readings. Each homework assignment is worth 5% of your final grade (25% cumulative). Due dates are on the course calendar.


Homework Grading
I will post solutions after each homework submission deadline. You are encouraged to self-grade your homework assignments using the posted solutions. Accurately self-grading each homework is 1% of your grade (5% cumulative). The grader and I will spot-check your self-grading, and you are encouraged to ask for help with self-grading during office hours.
Submit your self-graded homework solutions on Canvas one week after I post the solutions. Self-grading should include specific, detailed annotations on each sub-problem, marking:

where you made mistakes;
what your mistake was;
what a correct answer would have been.

In other words, give yourself the feedback that you think an ideal grader would give.
You are also welcome to opt out of self-grading, in whole or in part. If you do not complete your self-grading for an assignment by the corresponding deadline, we will assume that you want us to grade it for you.
All questions and objections to grading must be submitted in writing, as a private Canvas message to both me and the grader (see Communication).


Exams
The course has three in-class midterm exams, on the dates the course calendar lists. There is also an optional in-person final exam during finals week, at a time TBD. If a midterm’s date changes, I will announce the change at least two weeks before that exam is given.

I will provide a standardized note sheet for each exam.
Any calculator allowed for the SAT is allowed for the exams.
Midterms 1, 2 and 3 are worth 10%, 30% and 30% of the course grade.
I hold a review session before each exam.

The final exam is entirely optional. If your grade on the final is higher than the average of your three midterm grades, weighted 10 to 30 to 30, I will use your final grade to replace all three of your midterm grades. The final exam can only improve your grade.

Submitting Your Work
You will develop and store homework code in Git version control repositories. Specifically, we will use private GitHub repositories under a course GitHub organization (TBD). If you do not yet have a GitHub account, please create one. Be sure to push your final version before the assignment deadline: I will pull the current default branch of the repository at the due time. title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Program Guidelines
The grader and I will grade your programs on three criteria, in this order:

correctness;
clarity;
efficiency.

Correctness. A correct program produces the correct output for a given input, and does not produce unintended side effects. Test each component as you introduce it, and try to break your program in testing.
Clarity. The easier it is to read your code, the easier it is to find and remove bugs. Design your program thoughtfully and modularly, and replace two blocks of code that do the same thing with one function called from both places.
Efficiency. Your programs should be asymptotically efficient. Beyond that, use vectorized tensor operations and take advantage of the optimizations built into the libraries we use.

title: WWU CSCI 481 (Deep Learning) Syllabus
text:
Academic Honesty
As a future professional, your integrity is crucial. It is your responsibility to read and be familiar with the university’s academic dishonesty policy, found in Appendix D of the Western Washington University Course Catalog.

Homework: you may collaborate freely with your classmates, and you may use AI tools, such as ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot.
Exams: in-class exams are solo. Work alone, without help from anyone else and without AI tools or other devices; the only aids allowed are the provided note sheet and a calculator, as described under Exams.

Cheating on an exam will result in failing the course (grade of F), and I will file documentation of the incident with the university. When in doubt, ask the instructor.

Writing to Think
When you are stuck in this course, try putting your question into words in writing. Write it in full sentences, with the numbers or code you used and what you have already tried. In an interview on the 5 Minute Mentor podcast, Leslie Lamport says:

As someone said, “Writing is nature’s way of showing you how fuzzy your thinking is.” If you think you understand something, and don’t write down your ideas, you only think you’re thinking.
— Leslie Lamport [9]

title: Deep Learning
text:
This website collects the lecture notes for CSCI 481, “Deep Learning”, as taught in Spring Quarter 2027 at Western Washington University by Douglas Ezra Morrison.
The course follows the module sequence of Brian Hutchinson’s CSCI 481/581, which he taught from Winter 2021 to Winter 2026.
CSCI 481 builds on DATA 371/471, Machine Learning. Where these notes use an idea that course covers, such as generalization, gradient descent, or logistic regression, they link to its definition in Machine Learning for Data Science (lds) rather than defining it again.
The Calendar lists the topics week by week, and the Syllabus gives the course’s policies. The main reference text is Deep Learning [1], which can be read at no cost on the book’s webpage.




[1] I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio, and A. Courville, Deep learning. MIT Press, 2016. Available: https://www.deeplearningbook.org/

title: Calendar
text:
The topics and dates of future lectures may change.
Spring quarter runs from Tuesday, March 30 to Friday, June 11, 2027, with finals week from Monday, June 7 to Friday, June 11. Class meets on Mondays, Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays, 9:00–9:50am, in CF 420. There is no class on Monday, May 31, for Memorial Day.
Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays are lectures from these notes, apart from exam days and Memorial Day. Fridays are lab sessions, for working on the homework in class, except on the three Fridays that hold a midterm review.
Homework is due at 11:59 pm on its due date, always a Friday. Each self-grade is due one week after that homework’s solutions are posted. The self-grade dates below assume the solutions go up at the deadline.
The three midterms are in class:

Midterm 1, Monday, April 26: weeks 1 to 4, from the course overview through normalization and residual connections.
Midterm 2, Monday, May 17: convolutional networks, sequence models, language modeling, attention, and Transformers’ self-attention and positional encoding.
Midterm 3, Tuesday, June 1: the lectures from Transformer pretraining through running deep learning experiments.

Each midterm covers the lectures since the one before it, and has an in-class review session on the Friday before the exam.
The final exam is optional. Its day and time are still to be set (TBD): WWU’s finals schedule sets each exam’s slot from the class’s start time and meeting days. The final’s review session will be held during finals week, at a time TBD.
